title: Opening the Divan
hookLine: Iranians still open Hafiz at random for guidance, especially on the longest night, Yalda
tomorrow: a poet named for the Quran, writing about wine. how?

lines: A COIN, A GROUP CHAT, A BOOK.
TOO MUCH WINE FOR THE RITES?
cards: Some people flip a coin. Some ask the group chat. Inés, the day after the memorial, can't decide whether to go back to work on Monday, and she asks Zoe to open Hafiz for her.
In Shiraz, the story goes, the custom started at a coffin. Hafiz has died, and a crowd stands around his body, arguing. Some say a man who wrote that much about wine shouldn't get the full rites.

teach.b: Tradition says they settled it by letting Hafiz decide.

His verses were drawn at random, and the couplet that came up spoke to the mourners directly: don't hold back your step from Hafiz's bier, for though he's drowned in sin, he's on his way to paradise. So they buried him.
True or not, the legend explains a living custom. It's called fal-e Hafez.

teach.h: FAL-E HAFEZ: A LINE FOR A QUESTION.
teach.b: In Iran, people hold a question in their heart, open the Divan wherever it falls, and read that ghazal as a line for today.
Tradition gives him a title for it: Lisan al-Ghayb, the Tongue of the Unseen.
Families do it especially on Yalda, the longest night of the year, staying up late with fruit and nuts and reading Hafiz aloud to one another. Be honest about the edges.
Some Muslim scholars frown on it as fortune-telling; others treat it as a custom of Persian culture, not a prophecy.
Either way, the poem doesn't decide for you. It sits beside you while you decide. So Zoe opens the book for Inés, and reads her one ghazal, slowly.

how: In Iran, families practice fal-e Hafez: holding an intention, opening the Divan at random and reading that ghazal aloud, especially on Yalda night. Some Muslim scholars disapprove of it as divination; others treat it as a cultural custom.

games.why: fal-e Hafez gives you company for the question, not an answer to obey. the poem sits beside you while you decide.

practice: Take any book near you, hold a question lightly, and open it anywhere. Read only the first line your eyes land on. Sit with it for two minutes, not as an order, but as company.

orig.note: Persian: an omen, a reading. Fal-e Hafez is a reading taken from Hafiz's Divan.

carryVoice: Your line: a line for today, to sit with, not to obey. Two days into Hafiz.
